title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM + CUDA Graphs (Deep Dive)
summary: Redwood SE-led deep dive to review GPU runtime profiling for Quantify Labs' inference workloads. Focus on kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM throughput/latency, CUDA graphs stability, KV cache behavior, batching strategies and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem VPC deployment. Agreed to run a 48-hour benchmark on customer samples and share kernel-level flamegraphs + cudagraph traces.
action_items: Elena: share initial kernel selection spreadsheet and perf baseline by 2026-01-20
Alex: provide 3 representative prompt workloads + model checkpoints (huggingface s3 link) by 2026-01-19
Ravi: propose infra config for 48h benchmark (GPU types, NCCL settings) by 2026-01-21
next_steps: Run 48-hour perf run with TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on customer's prompts; compare p95 latency and throughput
Share CUDA Graph tracers, kernel flamegraphs, and batch histograms
Schedule follow-up to review results w/ eng + SRE (target 2026-01-27)
Send security docs for on-prem VPC deployment and KMS integration
transcript:
[00:00] Samir (AE): Okay everyone, thanks for carving out time. We're here to go deep on GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection, and the TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM comparison for your on-prem inference. Can we kick off with quick intros?
[00:12] Alex (Customer): yeah Alex from Quantify Labs, ML platform. Maya is SRE, Tom does model infra, Jules will jump in if needed.
[00:20] Elena (SE): Elena, Redwood SE, I own performance onboarding — happy to shadow with kernel-level profiling. Sorry if any audio glitches, I might drop & come back, internet's a bit flaky.
[00:30] Tom (Customer): cool. high level: we've got a mix of llm-13b and 33b variants, mostly 8k context, sometimes 32k. primary target is p95 latency under 200ms for single-turn inference when possible, and consistent throughput for batch scoring.
[00:45] Samir: good, helps set expectations. Are you leaning on on-prem GPUs or cloud instances?
[00:50] Maya: on-prem DGX-style pods, A100 and a couple H100 later this quarter. network is fat tree, but low tolerance for noisy neighbor. we want VPC-like isolation and key management on-prem.
[01:03] Elena: great — that maps to things we'll test. Today we'll show kernel selection impacts (memory layout, fused kernels), how CUDA graphs can reduce CPU overhead & jitter, and differences between TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels vs vLLM's fused attention and scheduling.
[01:20] Jules (CTO): quick question, do we expect cudagraphs to break KV cache hot reloads? we've seen issues in internal tests where graph capture caches stale pointers.
[01:30] Elena: yes that's a known class of problems. we instrumented captures to rebind KV pointers and use segmented captures; we'll show mitigations. sometimes you need per-sequence-length graphs or dynamic replays, which costs memory.
[01:45] Alex: can you quantify gains? like when is TensorRT-LLM better than vLLM?
[01:52] Elena: high level: TensorRT-LLM tends to win on steady-state high-throughput (large batch, long seq) because of kernel fusion & tensor cores optimized paths; vLLM often gives lower tail latency for varied small-batch, many-concurrent requests due to its dynamic scheduler and better CPU->GPU pipelining. numbers vary by model & quantization. e.g., for 13B int8 we saw 1.8x throughput with TRT-LLM on A100 for batch sizes > 16, but p95 latency at batch size 1 favored vLLM by ~20-30ms on some workloads.
[02:25] Tom: what about KV cache behavior for multi-turn chat? our bots do incremental decoding a lot.
[02:31] Elena: KV cache is critical. TensorRT-LLM stores KV in packed formats and uses fused gather-scatter which is fast, but cudagraphs can complicate incremental updates because capture assumes static memory layout. vLLM keeps a more flexible KV layout which helps for frequent prefix updates. Our approach is hybrid: use CUDA graphs for steady-state generation and fall back to dynamic paths when cache mutation rate is high.
[02:55] Maya: how do you detect when to fall back? automated heuristics?
[03:00] Elena: we instrument request patterns. heuristics include prefix-change rate, tokens-per-request, and cold-start frequency. If prefix-change > X% per minute we route to dynamic runtime. Also we can compile per-common-prefix graphs if there are stable dialogs.
[03:18] Samir: can we talk a bit about kernel selection — what do you tune?
[03:22] Elena: yes — kernel selection includes choosing fused attention vs vanilla matmul-attn, block sizes, using Tensor Cores (mixed precision), and custom fused softmax/backward kernels. Also memory layout (NCHW-like vs custom) matters for bandwidth. We profile with nvprof / Nsight and our own kernel flamegraphs.
[03:40] Tom: we attempted INT8 quantization with HuggingFace QAT and saw quality regressions. is 4-bit feasible?
[03:47] Elena: 4-bit (QLoRA-style) can work for many models but needs calibration. TensorRT's int8 calibration is pretty robust, but for 4-bit you often rely on quantization-aware fine-tuning or post-training quant with per-channel scales. Expect some eval metric drop — we recommend rolling evals against your prompt suites. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload.
[04:08] Alex: CUDA graphs: what are common pitfalls?
[04:12] Elena: pitfalls: stale pointer captures (Jules' case), varying sequence length -> leads to many graphs, graph replay overhead for small batches, and issues with NCCL comms when graphs include collective ops. We mitigate by: segmented graphs, parameterized graph templates, and replay-only graphs for generation loops while keeping KV mutations outside captured region.
[04:36] Maya: NCCL issues — we saw deadlocks during scaling. is there a recommended pattern?
[04:41] Elena: yes avoid capturing NCCL collective ops inside a graph that will be replayed asynchronously across different streams. Instead, separate all NCCL setup/teardown from the capture and use point-to-point kernels in capture. Ensure stream synchronization is explicit. Also ensure driver versions and CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT versions are pinned — mismatches cause weird hangs.
[04:58] Tom: performance numbers, can you show a concrete benchmark?
[05:02] Elena: sure — we pulled a quick baseline for a 13B model, 8k context. On A100, batch sizes: 1 -> vLLM p95 120ms, TRT-LLM p95 140ms; batch 16 -> TRT-LLM throughput 3.2x vLLM and average latency comparable. With int8 quant, TRT-LLM improved throughput further but had slightly higher p95 for rare tokens.
[05:30] Alex: ok that's helpful. How do you capture kernel traces for us to investigate?
[05:34] Elena: we produce: cudagraph trace logs, kernel flamegraphs (text + svg), kernel timing histograms, and a batch distribution CSV. We'll share the bundle. For privacy we'll scrub any customer prompt text unless you want us to keep it.
[05:50] Jules: for on-prem, KMS & SSO are blockers for legal. what's Redwood's story?
[05:55] Samir: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, audit logs and per-tenant RBAC. We'll send our security packet and SOC2 evidence.
[06:05] Maya: one more on memory — we've hit OOM with 32k contexts on 33B even with offloading. any guidance?
[06:12] Elena: strategies: KV sharding across GPUs, activation offload, quantization, and dynamic tensor eviction. Offloading has latency cost. Also split attention kernels (chunked attention) trade memory for compute. We'll include recommended configs per GPU type.
[06:30] Alex: can Redwood run the benchmark on our cluster? we can give SRE access for 48hrs.
[06:36] Samir: yes we can run a co-managed run: we'll bring a small Redwood team, run TensorRT-LLM and vLLM binaries, collect traces, and hand back artifacts. Need the sample prompts and model artifacts.
[06:50] Tom: licensing — TRT-LLM requires TensorRT licensing?
[06:53] Elena: TensorRT is NVIDIA-provided, free to use but does require compatible driver stack; some enterprise features tie to NVIDIA enterprise subscriptions. We can enumerate exact reqs in a doc.
[07:05] Maya: any quick wins to reduce p95 now?
[07:08] Elena: reduce cold-starts by warm pools (poolsize), enable prefix caching for common prompts, use cudagraphs for generation hot paths, and apply conservative quantization (int8) for heavy throughput paths. Also tune batching window to balance latency/throughput.
[07:25] Samir: ok circling back, action items are to exchange artifacts and run the 48h perf job. we'll target next review 2026-01-27. anything else?
[07:34] Alex: send kernel-level outputs and security docs. Also please include a short README for reproducing the runs.
[07:40] Samir: noted. thanks everyone.
[07:45] (call ends)
notes: Transcript has occasional mis-attributions and small transcription errors; attendees agreed to a co-managed 48h benchmark and exchange of kernel-level artifacts. Security docs and onboarding steps to follow.
